pages.name: Still there?
pages.task: A transformer has an R% of 1.5 and an X% of 3. At full load, 0.8 lagging, its output sags 3.0%. At 0.8 leading, the same current lifts its output by 0.6%. Why the difference?
pages.answer: The angle turns the same drops along or against the output
pages.why: The windings drop the same size of voltage at both loads. Lagging, the reactance's drop lines up with the output and comes straight off: 1.5 × 0.8 + 3 × 0.6 = 3.0%. Leading, it swings round against the output: 1.2 − 1.8 = −0.6%. A generator does the same, through its own reactance.
options: The leading load draws less current
The leading load meets less resistance
The angle turns the same drops along or against the output

pages.name: One phase
pages.text: Each phase works like a voltage inside, E, in series with the synchronous reactance, Xs. 100% field makes 1.0 per unit with nothing connected. Then no current flows and V equals E. On load, the current drops voltage across Xs. Then E and V part.

pages.name: The drop in volts
pages.task: This set's Xs is 1.5 per unit. Per unit is a fraction of the set's own rating. So 1.0 means 440 V between lines, or rated current. Rated current flows. How big is the drop across Xs, as a line voltage?
pages.why: The drop is Xs × I = 1.5 × 1.0 = 1.5 per unit. As a line voltage that is 1.5 × 440 = 660 V. The drop inside is bigger than the voltage at the terminals.

pages.text: At unity, the drop stands at right angles to V from its tip. E closes the triangle. It is 1.80 per unit, 56° ahead of V. With Xs at 0.1, E is barely longer than V.

pages.name: Half the current
pages.task: At unity, the load falls to half rated current, 0.5 per unit. Xs is 1.5 and the AVR holds V at 1.0. How big must E be?
pages.why: The drop is 1.5 × 0.5 = 0.75, at right angles to V. E = √(1.0² + 0.75²) = √1.5625 = 1.25.

pages.name: Which needs more field
pages.task: Predict before you look. Two loads draw rated current from the set. One is at 0.8 lagging and one is at 0.8 leading. The AVR holds V at 1.0. Which needs more field current?
pages.why: A lagging current tips the drop forward along V. A leading one tips it back against V. So on the lagging load E must reach further, and the field makes E. The next screens work out how much further.

pages.name: A leading load
pages.text: At 0.8 leading, the drop leans back. E's part along V falls to 0.1. E falls to 1.20. On a Zero pf leading load the whole drop points back against V. Enough current takes the field to zero. The diodes on the shaft pass current one way only, so the field cannot reverse. Then V climbs.

pages.name: Field to zero
pages.task: A set feeds only correction capacitors, left in after the rest of the load has gone. That is a Zero pf leading load. Xs is 1.5 and the AVR holds V at 1.0. At what current does the field reach zero?
pages.why: E = 1.0 − 1.5 × I. That is zero when I = 1.0 ÷ 1.5 = 0.67 per unit. So two-thirds of rated current, all of it leading, leaves the AVR nothing to cut. A real set can lose control sooner, even on a slightly leading load.

pages.name: The AVR off
pages.text: With the AVR off, the field and E keep their lengths. At the same current, a 0.8 lagging load shrinks V, and a 0.8 leading load raises it.

pages.name: V with the AVR off
pages.task: With the AVR on at unity and rated current, the field sat at 180% and E at 1.80. The AVR is now off. The same current swings to 0.8 lagging. E's part across V is 1.2 and the drop's part along V is 0.9. What is V now?
pages.why: E keeps its length, 1.80. Its part across V is 1.2. So its part along V is √(3.24 − 1.44) = √1.80 = 1.34. The drop takes 0.9 of that. So V = 1.34 − 0.9 = 0.44. On the same current, V has fallen by more than half.

pages.name: The load angle
pages.task: Rated current flows at 0.8 lagging. Xs is 1.5 and the AVR holds V at 1.0. What is the load angle δ between E and V?
pages.why: Along V: 1.0 + 0.9 = 1.9. Across V: 1.2. tan δ = 1.2 ÷ 1.9 = 0.63. So δ = 32°. E runs 32° ahead of V. This angle matters again when sets share load.

pages.name: The rating
pages.task: Sets are rated at 0.8 power factor. So the winding and the field are built for rated current at 0.8 lagging, as drawn here. A 630 kVA set runs at 440 V between lines. What line current flows at its full rating?
pages.why: I = 630 000 ÷ (√3 × 440) = 630 000 ÷ 762.1 = 826.7 A. At 0.8 the set gives 630 × 0.8 = 504 kW. Its winding must carry 826.7 A at 0.8 lagging, and its field must make the larger E that needs. A load that lags more asks for more field than the set was built to give.
